# Judith Chapter 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Judith 14

---

**1** Judith said to them, "Listen to me now, my brothers. Take this head and hang it on the parapet of your wall.

**2** As soon as morning breaks and the sun rises over the earth, let every man take up his weapons of war, and let every able-bodied man march out of the city. Appoint a commander over them as though you were going down to the plain against the Assyrian advance guard — but do not go down.

**3** They will take up their arms, go to their camp, and rouse the officers of the Assyrian army. They will run to the tent of Holofernes and not find him. Fear will come over them and they will flee before you.

**4** Then you and all who live throughout the territory of Israel will pursue them and cut them down in their tracks.

**5** But before you do this, call Achior the Ammonite to me, so that he may see and acknowledge the man who treated the house of Israel with contempt and sent him to us as though to his death."

**6** They called Achior from the house of Uzziah. When he came and saw the head of Holofernes held in the hand of a man in the assembly of the people, he fell on his face and his spirit failed him.

**7** When they helped him up, he fell at the feet of Judith and bowed down before her, saying, "Blessed are you in every tent of Judah, and in every nation — all who hear your name will be filled with dread.

**8** Now tell me everything you have done in these days." And Judith told him, in the hearing of all the people, everything she had done. When she finished speaking, the people raised a great shout and filled the city with rejoicing.

**9** When Achior saw all that the God of Israel had done, he believed in God wholeheartedly and had himself circumcised, and he was incorporated into the house of Israel — and so it has remained to this day.

**10** As soon as morning dawned, they hung the head of Holofernes on the wall. Every man took up his weapons and they went out in companies to the slopes of the mountain.

**11** When the Assyrians saw them, they sent word to their commanders, who in turn went to the generals, the captains, and all the officers.

**12** They came to Holofernes' tent and said to the one in charge of all his affairs, "Wake up our master — for the slaves have dared to march down against us to give battle, to their own destruction."

**13** Bagoas went in and knocked on the door of the tent, supposing that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith.

**14** But when no one answered, he opened it and went into the bedchamber and found him thrown on the threshold, dead, with his head taken from him.

**15** He cried out with a loud voice and wept and moaned and shouted and tore his garments.

**16** Then he went into the tent where Judith had been lodging and did not find her; and he rushed out to the troops and cried,

**17** "The slaves have been treacherous! One Hebrew woman has brought disgrace upon the house of King Nebuchadnezzar! Holofernes is lying on the ground — and his head is gone from him!"

**18** When the officers of the Assyrian army heard these words, they tore their garments, and a terrible dread came over them, and throughout the camp there arose a cry and a great outcry.

**19** And the men in their tents, when they heard it, were horrified at what had taken place.

---

### Council Notes

**On verse 5 — Achior's role:** Achior first appeared in ch. 5-6, where he told Holofernes that Israel could not be conquered unless they sinned against their God. Holofernes was furious, banished him to Bethulia, and left him to share Israel's fate. The author now completes the narrative arc: Achior is brought to see the vindication of his own speech.

**On verse 6 — "his spirit failed him":** All three agents treat exepsychē as a fainting episode, not death. This is contextually correct — the next verse has him speaking. The verb is ambiguous in Greek but the narrative clarifies it.

**On verse 9 — Achior's conversion:** This is one of the most theologically significant moments in the deuterocanonical literature. An Ammonite — a member of a people explicitly excluded from the assembly of Israel in Deuteronomy 23:3 — converts and is circumcised. The author treats this without any anxiety about the prohibition. Grace supersedes exclusion. PNEUMA notes correctly that Achior's entire story arc is completed here: he who spoke truth is vindicated and joins the people whose God he vindicated.

**On verse 9 — "believed in God wholeheartedly":** Greek episteuse sphodra tō theō — "believed greatly/intensely." The word sphodra (greatly, strongly) is emphatic. LOGOS' "wholeheartedly" and PNEUMA's "deeply, completely" both capture it. SOPHIA uses "wholeheartedly" as a single adverb that conveys the totality.

**On verse 13 — Bagoas' assumption:** This is the devastating irony of the chapter. Every detail Judith constructed — the nighttime absences for prayer, the fiction that she was being seduced into Holofernes' bed — has led to this moment where Bagoas knocks on the door of a dead man.

**On verse 14 — "thrown on the threshold":** The Greek keitai epi tou edaphous — "lying on the floor." The threshold detail appears in some readings. SOPHIA retains "threshold" as the more specific reading, which heightens the indignity: he was not laid out on his bed but found crumpled at the floor near the entrance.

**On verse 17 — Bagoas' announcement:** "One Hebrew woman" — the emphasis is meant to compound the shame in Assyrian eyes. The most powerful general in the empire, defeated by a single woman. The author wants this humiliation to sting.
